newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark's Lykketoft says share tax plan not dead.
newsitem.headline: Denmark's Lykketoft says share tax plan not dead.

text.p: Danish Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft says that he has not abandoned his plan to tax yields of pension-related shareholdings, shelved last month in the battle to win parliamentary backing for the 1997 budget.

Writing in his Social Democratic Party newspaper on Thursday he said that a fresh attempt to introduce the tax -- likely to depress share prices -- could be made during the current parliament or after general elections scheduled for 1998.
"I believe that these tax changes will be on the political agenda and brought to life within the next two to four years," he wrote.
The scheme would tax the yields of shares held by pension funds, insurance companies or as part of private pension plans, in order to finance a cut in corporation tax.

Danish analysts say that should the plan be introduced, local institutional buyers will still seek much the same returns after tax, driving down prices on the Copenhagen bourse but providing paper at a discount to tax-exempt foreign investors.
The mere possibility of such a tax was cited in November as contributing to falls in stock and bond prices.
Government planners say that the levy would be offset by growth stimulated by the accompanying cut in company tax.

Economists and political analysts doubt that the scheme will ever reach fruition, given the centre-left minority government's vulnerability in parliament and low approval rating in a series of recent polls.

"There is such hostility toward the (ruling) coalition from both the left and right in parliament that they won't try it anytime soon, they won't try it ahead of the September '98 elections and they most probably won't be in office afterward," a diplomat told Reuters.
